Positional encoding schemes — whether sinusoidal, learned absolute, or relative — are trained over a fixed context window, and the central question is: when inference-time sequences exceed that window, do attention logits remain well-calibrated, or do they distort in ways that collapse token-to-token information routing? The beginner assumes extrapolation fails gracefully, producing merely noisier outputs; the expert knows the failure mode is sharper — attention scores computed at unseen position indices can become extreme outliers, causing softmax to either saturate (near-one-hot collapse onto a single token) or diffuse (near-uniform attention that destroys locality), depending on how the positional signal enters the dot-product computation. With RoPE specifically, the rotation frequencies at high position indices produce phase interference patterns never seen during training, causing the effective "distance" between tokens to become non-monotonic — a token 2000 positions away may receive higher attention than one 50 positions away, violating the inductive bias the model learned to rely on. ALiBi sidesteps the rotation problem by adding a learned linear position bias rather than encoding position in the query-key space, but it introduces its own failure mode: the linear penalty slope calibrated for short sequences underestimates how much long-range attention should be suppressed at OOD lengths, leading to spurious long-range dependencies. What experts lose sleep over — and beginners never think to check — is that these failures are not uniform across heads: some attention heads extrapolate acceptably while others catastrophically distort, so aggregate perplexity metrics look deceptively healthy while specific capabilities (e.g., coreference resolution, instruction following across long contexts) silently degrade.

RoPE encodes position by rotating query and vector pairs in 2D subspaces using frequencies θ_i = 10000^(-2i/d), where i indexes the dimension pair — high-frequency components (small i, θ near 1) complete a full rotation cycle in very few positions, while low-frequency components (large i, θ near 10000^(-1)) rotate slowly across the entire training context. At OOD positions beyond training length L, high-frequency components have already cycled through many full rotations within training and now land at phase angles that were seen repeatedly but always in the context of short-range token pairs; at position L+k, those components produce dot-product contributions identical to some in-distribution position p < L, but the surrounding token context is entirely different, creating a systematic aliasing problem. The dot product between rotated queries and keys decomposes into a sum over these 2D subspace contributions, and because high-frequency subspaces alias aggressively, their contribution to the attention logit becomes essentially noise at OOD lengths — empirically, Chen et al. (2023, "Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation") show that naively extrapolating LLaMA beyond 2048 tokens causes perplexity to spike catastrophically, while interpolation recovers near-nominal perplexity after only 1000 fine-tuning steps. Position Interpolation addresses this by scaling all position indices by a factor L/L' (where L' is the target context length), mapping OOD positions back into [0, L] — this keeps every rotation component, including high-frequency ones, within the phase range the model has seen, at the cost of compressing the positional resolution and making nearby tokens slightly harder to distinguish. The insight motivating YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) is that uniform interpolation is wasteful: low-frequency components extrapolate acceptably on their own and don't need interpolation, so selectively interpolating only high-frequency components (those most prone to aliasing) while leaving low-frequency ones untouched preserves both long-range positional signal and fine-grained local distinctions simultaneously. The deeper expert concern is that interpolation is a patch over a mismatched inductive bias: RoPE's frequency design was chosen for elegant relative-position encoding within a fixed window, not for smooth extension, so any interpolation scheme is trading one distortion (aliasing) for another (resolution compression) without resolving the root mismatch.

YaRN's boundary is determined by a wavelength threshold: for each RoPE frequency component i, the wavelength λ_i = 2π/θ_i is compared against the original training context length L — components where λ_i < L are deemed to have completed enough cycles during training to suffer aliasing at extension, and are interpolated, while components where λ_i ≥ L are treated as safely extrapolatable because they haven't completed a full cycle and thus haven't built up aliasing artifacts. This criterion is theoretically motivated (wavelength relative to context is a principled measure of how much phase aliasing has accumulated) but the specific threshold value is not derived from first principles — Peng et al. set it heuristically and validate it empirically by sweeping context extension ratios and measuring perplexity on long-document benchmarks like PG-19 and SCROLLS, finding that the wavelength-relative boundary outperforms uniform interpolation but without a proof that it is optimal. A ramp function is also introduced in YaRN to smooth the transition between fully interpolated and fully extrapolated components rather than applying a hard cutoff, and the slope of that ramp (controlled by hyperparameters α and β) is likewise tuned empirically on the target extension ratio — so the method contains at least two calibration knobs whose settings are benchmark-specific and may not transfer across model families or extension ratios. If the boundary is set too conservatively (too many components interpolated), positional resolution collapses for nearby tokens — the model loses ability to distinguish position 1 from position 3, degrading tasks like counting, syntax parsing, and anything requiring precise local order. If the boundary is set too aggressively (too few components interpolated), high-frequency aliasing persists at the extended positions, manifesting as retrieval failures in needle-in-a-haystack evaluations where the model must locate a specific fact at position L+k and instead attends to a spuriously similar in-distribution position — a failure mode that perplexity metrics are essentially blind to because perplexity averages over all tokens and the aliased positions are sparse.

The sharpest diagnostic is the "needle-in-a-haystack" (NIAH) protocol, popularized by Kamradt (2023) and later systematized by teams evaluating GPT-4 and Claude, which plants a single retrievable fact at a controlled absolute position within a long filler context and measures exact-match retrieval accuracy as a function of both document depth (where in the context the needle sits) and total context length — this produces a 2D accuracy heatmap that directly exposes position-specific failures invisible to perplexity. The critical refinement that stress-tests aliasing specifically is varying needle position across the OOD boundary: a well-calibrated model should show smooth accuracy degradation as position increases past L, but an aliasing-afflicted model shows non-monotonic accuracy — positions that alias to high-attention in-distribution indices retrieve correctly while adjacent positions fail, producing a characteristic striped failure pattern in the heatmap whose spatial frequency corresponds to the wavelength of the aliased RoPE component. SCROLLS and LongBench are the most used long-context benchmarks, but both measure aggregate task accuracy over full documents rather than position-controlled retrieval, making them poor at localizing aliasing artifacts — a model can score 70% on LongBench's summarization tasks while completely failing retrieval at positions between 8k and 12k if the failure is sparse enough. BABILong (Kuratov et al., 2024) is more targeted, embedding reasoning facts at controlled positions within up to 1M token contexts, and reveals that most models including extended-RoPE variants collapse to near-random performance past 32k even when perplexity remains low — but it doesn't isolate the positional aliasing mechanism from other failure modes like attention sink formation or KV cache eviction. The honest expert assessment is that no current public benchmark cleanly isolates positional aliasing as a cause: what's needed is a protocol that holds semantic content constant, varies only the absolute position of the needle across a fine-grained grid spanning the OOD boundary, and reports per-position accuracy with enough trials to estimate variance — this exists in internal evaluations at labs but hasn't been released as a standardized community benchmark.

The intervention is therefore a controlled swap: keep the needle at a fixed absolute position but systematically vary the density and placement of sink-attracting tokens in the filler context — if retrieval accuracy changes significantly with sink token density but not with needle position modulo RoPE wavelength, sinks are the dominant mechanism; if accuracy correlates with (needle_position mod λ_i) for specific frequency components i but is insensitive to sink density, aliasing dominates. A complementary behavioral probe is the "duplicate needle" experiment: plant two semantically identical needles at positions p1 (in-distribution) and p2 (OOD), then ask the model to report both — aliasing predicts the model will confuse p2 with p1 and report p1 twice, while sink-driven failure predicts the model simply loses p2 without the confabulation artifact, since sink attention drains signal uniformly rather than redirecting it to a specific aliased position. Mechanistic dissociation without attention weight access is feasible but requires enough trials to estimate the spatial autocorrelation of failure across positions — aliasing produces failures with a characteristic period matching RoPE wavelengths (computable from model config), while sink failures produce failures that correlate with local sink token count rather than absolute position. With attention weight access, the dissociation is immediate: aliasing manifests as anomalously high attention scores between the query at the OOD needle position and keys at the aliased in-distribution position, while sinks manifest as high attention mass concentrated on a small set of structurally special tokens with near-zero residual for the needle token regardless of position — Xiao et al. Whether aliasing produces confabulation versus silent omission is determined by the strength of the aliased attention signal relative to the model's residual stream representation of the correct answer: if the aliased position p1 contains a token whose key vector is sufficiently similar to what the query at p2 expects — because p2's rotated query happens to align well with p1's rotated key after aliasing — the model actively retrieves p1's content and generates it confidently, producing confabulation; if the aliased position contains an unrelated token whose key doesn't match the query well even after aliasing, the attention signal at p2 diffuses across many positions and the residual stream receives no strong positional signal, producing omission. The critical moderating variable is therefore semantic coherence of the aliased landing position: in RAG pipelines where documents are chunked and concatenated, aliasing is especially dangerous because the filler context is semantically rich and topically related to the query, dramatically increasing the probability that the aliased position p1 contains plausible-but-wrong content that passes the model's implicit relevance check and gets confidently retrieved. Confabulation is strictly more dangerous than omission in RAG settings because standard faithfulness evaluations — including RAG-specific benchmarks like RAGAS and TruLens scoring — check whether the model's output is entailed by some retrieved chunk, but a confabulated answer citing content from p1 will score as faithful if p1 exists in the context, even though the correct answer was at p2 and was never actually retrieved. The aliasing-to-confabulation pathway is also self-concealing in production: the model generates a fluent, citation-supported answer with high confidence, so neither automated scoring nor casual human review flags it — only a protocol that explicitly tracks which chunk position was accessed, rather than what content was generated, would catch it. Empirically, this failure mode is structurally analogous to the "lost in the middle" phenomenon documented by Liu et al. (2023), where models preferentially retrieve from early and late context positions, but aliasing introduces an additional failure layer where the retrieval appears successful (a specific position is attended to) while being positionally incorrect — making it harder to detect than simple recency or primacy bias.

Position-tagged attention — augmenting the attention mechanism to log which absolute positions contributed most to each generated token — is implementable as an inference-time wrapper without architectural changes, and systems like Anthropic's citation mechanism and perplexity.ai's source highlighting approximate this by identifying which retrieved chunk maps to each output span; but these operate at chunk granularity, not token-position granularity, so aliasing within a chunk (where p2 aliases to p1 within the same document) is invisible to them. A stronger architectural intervention is explicit source-position grounding in the generation objective: training the model to generate a position tag alongside each factual claim, as in Guo et al.'s (2022) attributed question answering work, forces the model to commit to a specific retrieval location — if the committed position is p1 but the correct answer is at p2, the discrepancy becomes detectable by a verifier with access to the original document. The displacement problem is real and sharp, however: a model trained to emit position tags will learn to emit whichever position tag minimizes training loss, which during aliasing is the position the model actually attended to (p1), not the correct position (p2) — so the tag is self-consistent with the model's (wrong) internal retrieval but inconsistent with ground truth, meaning the tag confirms the confabulation rather than exposing it. A more promising inference-time intervention is attention head ablation probing: at OOD positions, selectively zero out the high-frequency RoPE components known to alias (identified from the model's frequency spectrum) and measure whether the retrieved content changes — if ablating those components causes the model to either retrieve correctly from p2 or fall back to omission, you've confirmed aliasing as the mechanism and simultaneously identified which heads are responsible. The honest assessment is that none of these interventions solve the detection problem cleanly because they all share a common dependency: they require either knowing the correct retrieval position a priori (which defeats the purpose of RAG) or having a verifier that can distinguish p1-consistent from p2-consistent answers independently of the generator — and in practice, that verifier is either another LLM (which may itself alias) or a human (who cannot scale to production volumes).

Aliasing errors between generator and verifier will correlate strongly when both models share the same base RoPE configuration — identical θ_i frequencies and training context length L produce identical aliasing periodicity, meaning both models misattend to the same set of in-distribution positions at the same OOD offsets, creating a systematic blind spot where the verifier confidently endorses exactly the confabulations the generator produces. Decorrelation is achievable in principle by pairing models with different training context lengths (e.g., a 4k-trained generator with a 32k-trained verifier), because the aliasing period for component i scales with L — a position that aliases in the 4k model maps to a non-aliasing in-distribution position in the 32k model, so the verifier attends correctly where the generator confabulates. However, this decorrelation is incomplete: the low-frequency RoPE components that both models share (since θ_i for large i is nearly identical regardless of L) will still produce correlated errors at very long OOD positions, and the high-frequency components only decorrelate within a band determined by the ratio L_verifier/L_generator — outside that band, even the 32k verifier begins aliasing and the two models reconverge on the same wrong retrieval. Ensemble-based detection strategies that pool multiple verifiers with diverse RoPE configurations (varying both L and the base frequency 10000, as in models that use base frequencies of 500k like LLaMA-3) can reduce systematic blind spots, but the ensemble's reliability is bounded by the coverage of the aliasing phase space — if all ensemble members are drawn from the same model family with similar architectural choices, their aliasing patterns will partially overlap even with different L values, producing correlated failure clusters rather than independent errors. The deeper implication is that ensemble diversity for aliasing detection needs to be architectural rather than merely parametric: mixing RoPE models with ALiBi models, or with models using learned absolute positions, provides genuine independence because their failure modes are mechanistically distinct — ALiBi's linear penalty doesn't alias periodically, so an ALiBi verifier's errors are structurally uncorrelated with RoPE confabulations, making it a genuinely complementary signal rather than a noisy copy.
